extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students of literature, poets and writers interested in Romantic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and application of Percy Bysshe Shelley's essays (collection: A Defence of Poetry and Other Essays) to creative-writing practice and literary analysis. The text offers philosophical reflections on love, life, imagination, punishment, and the mind that can be used as evaluative principles for poetic and persuasive writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love as a creative-sympathetic impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is that powerful attraction towards all that we conceive, or fear, or hope beyond ourselves… If we imagine, we would that the airy children of our brain were born anew within another's… This is Love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley's description treats love as the impulse to make internal imaginings shared and real in others; for creative writing, aim to render internal images so vividly that readers 'recognize' and empathize with them. The passage elaborates on components (ideal prototype, sympathy, matching nerves/eyes) as the aim toward which love (and by analogy, art) strives. Anti-pattern: writing that isolates private visions without striving to awaken corresponding feeling in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural imagery to evoke inner states
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hence in solitude… we love the flowers, the grass, and the waters, and the sky. In the motion of the very leaves of spring… There is eloquence in the tongueless wind, and a melody in the flowing brooks…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley recommends employing nature's sights and sounds as a language to mirror and awaken interior feeling. Practical guidance: allow landscape and natural detail to carry emotional meaning rather than relying solely on explicit statement. Example: using the 'rustling of the reeds' to produce 'tears of mysterious tenderness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to create wonder by conceiving the previously unperceived
rubrics_metrics.description: “If any artist… had painted to us… the spectacle now afforded by the nightly cope of heaven… great would be our admiration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original imaginative creation — presenting scenes, systems, or images not previously perceived by the audience — produces astonishment and admiration. For writers: prioritize inventive, large-scale imaginative acts (new metaphors, striking visions) that make readers see the familiar as if for the first time. Anti-pattern: merely reiterating commonplace description that fails to produce astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words are limited but can illuminate ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: “How vain is it to think that words can penetrate the mystery of our being! Rightly used they may make evident our ignorance to ourselves, and this is much.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley acknowledges linguistic limits yet assigns a valuable role to language: to clarify, to reveal limits of understanding, and to provoke thought. Guidance for writers: use language to interrogate rather than to falsely resolve mystery; embrace ambiguity when appropriate. Scoring note: clarity that exposes depth is preferable to false precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination composes from perception: think only what is perceived
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is an axiom in mental philosophy, that we can think of nothing which we have not perceived. … The most astonishing combinations of poetry… are no other than combinations which the intellect makes of sensations according to its own laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley frames creative invention as recombination of perceived sensations. For practice: ground imaginative leaps in sensory detail and memory; novel combinations of concrete perceptions yield credible imagination. Anti-pattern: abstract invention lacking sensory anchoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry and rhetoric should foster sympathy and reformation, not revenge
rubrics_metrics.description: In discussing capital punishment Shelley argues that spectacle and revenge 'excite those emotions which it is the chief object of civilization to extinguish' and that punishment should aim at 'reformation and the restraint of those who transgress the laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For persuasive and political writing, avoid rhetoric that gratifies vengeance or cruelty; instead cultivate arguments that appeal to reform, social betterment, and humane sentiments. Example: when depicting suffering, aim to produce empathy and civic reflection rather than vindictive delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the reader's habit of familiarity to restore wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mist of familiarity obscures from us the wonder of our being… The multitude of men care not for them. It is thus with Life—that which includes all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley advises writers to counter readers' habituation by re-presenting ordinary things in a way that renews wonder. Practical technique: defamiliarization — framing common objects or experiences with fresh perspective, intensified detail, or unexpected analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of philosophical tone: avoid seduction by facile systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Shelley critiques materialism as 'a seducing system to young and superficial minds' that 'dispenses them from thinking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When incorporating philosophy into creative or critical writing, beware of simplistic doctrines that short-circuit inquiry. Value nuanced, reflective positions that acknowledge complexity. Anti-pattern: adopting fashionable but intellectually lazy frameworks for rhetorical effect.
